title: Iron Deficiency vs Anemia of Inflammation: Empty or Locked Stores
summary: Separate iron deficiency anemia from anemia of inflammation (chronic disease) by reading iron stores: ferritin, transferrin/TIBC, RDW and marrow iron, and learn why an inflamed patient’s normal ferritin can hide iron deficiency.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 9 Hit 1 (IDA vs ACD iron-study split), Trap 1 (normal ferritin in obvious iron deficiency) and the Figure 9 memory anchor (IDA = low ferritin, high RDW, empty stores; ACD = normal-to-high ferritin, normal RDW, locked stores). Checked against Nairz 2016, Iolascon 2024 (EHA-associated recommendations, which summarize the WHO 2020 ferritin thresholds), Kumar 2022, Tefferi 2005 and D’Angelo 2013. Qualifications: the reviewer calls both anemias microcytic, while Nairz 2016 describes anemia of inflammation as typically mild-to-moderate normocytic and only sometimes microcytic (register flag rv-acd-normocytic-ch9); Trap 1’s dodge pairs ferritin with RDW and iron studies, while the open sources adjust the ferritin threshold for inflammation (CRP), use transferrin saturation and sTfR/log ferritin (register flag rv-ferritin-inflammation-ch9). The RDW reference interval in the Number Vault is not taught. The WHO ferritin guideline itself was not opened in this session; its thresholds are cited as summarized by Iolascon 2024.

objectives: Explain why serum iron and transferrin saturation cannot separate iron deficiency from anemia of inflammation.
Contrast ferritin, transferrin/TIBC, RDW, red-cell size and marrow iron in the two conditions.
Recognise when inflammation can mask iron deficiency and which tests help (CRP, adjusted ferritin threshold, sTfR/log ferritin).

scenes.title: Same low iron, three stories
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three anemic adults, all with low serum iron and low transferrin saturation. (A) A woman with heavy menstrual bleeding: microcytic, ferritin 8 µg/L. (B) A man with active rheumatoid arthritis: ferritin 400 µg/L, C-reactive protein high. (C) A woman with active Crohn disease: ferritin 60 µg/L, C-reactive protein high. Question token: “Empty stores or locked stores?”

cues.text: Three anemic adults. All three have low serum iron and low transferrin saturation.
One has heavy periods and a very low ferritin. One has active arthritis and a high ferritin. One has active Crohn disease and a ferritin that looks normal.
Are their iron stores empty, or full but locked away?

scenes.title: Where iron lives
scenes.altText: Schematic iron-traffic diagram. Transferrin carries iron in plasma to the marrow for hemoglobin. Ferritin is the storage protein; in the absence of inflammation serum ferritin tracks total body iron stores. Macrophages in liver and spleen recycle iron from old red cells. Hepcidin, raised by inflammation, blocks iron release from macrophages and iron absorption from the gut, diverting iron into storage sites. Transferrin is a negative acute-phase reactant; ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant.

cues.text: Iron travels in plasma on transferrin, which delivers it to the marrow to build hemoglobin.
Spare iron is stored with ferritin. Without inflammation, serum ferritin tracks the body’s total iron stores closely.
Inflammation raises hepcidin. Hepcidin blocks iron release from macrophages and blocks absorption from the gut, so iron is diverted into storage and the marrow goes short.
Inflammation also shifts the carriers: ferritin is a positive acute-phase protein that rises, and transferrin is a negative one that falls.

scenes.title: Empty stores vs locked stores
scenes.altText: Side-by-side pattern cards. Iron deficiency anemia (empty stores): serum iron low, transferrin saturation low, ferritin low, transferrin/TIBC raised, RDW raised, microcytic hypochromic. Anemia of inflammation / chronic disease (locked stores): serum iron low, transferrin saturation low, ferritin normal or high, transferrin/TIBC normal or low, RDW typically normal, usually mild-to-moderate normocytic but can be microcytic. Marrow card: absent stainable marrow iron is the traditional gold standard for absolute iron deficiency; in functional (inflammatory) iron deficiency stainable iron is present unless absolute deficiency coexists; marrow is not done routinely.

cues.text: Both conditions show low serum iron and low transferrin saturation, so those two tests cannot separate them. The stores can.
Iron deficiency means empty stores: ferritin low, transferrin and TIBC raised as the body hunts for iron, red cells small and pale, and the RDW raised.

Anemia of inflammation means locked stores: ferritin normal or high, transferrin and TIBC normal or low, RDW typically normal. It is usually a mild to moderate normocytic anemia, though it can be microcytic.
The traditional gold standard is a marrow iron stain: no stainable iron in absolute deficiency, iron present when it is only locked away. Marrow sampling is invasive and is not done routinely.

props.label: Marrow iron: absent = empty · present = locked (not routine)

scenes.title: When inflammation hides iron deficiency
scenes.altText: Ferritin-in-inflammation card: because ferritin is an acute-phase protein, inflammation can push it into the normal range even when stores are low. Check C-reactive protein; when inflammation is present, use a higher ferritin threshold — WHO thresholds as summarized by Iolascon 2024: below 70 µg/L in adults with inflammation (WHO 2020), below 15 µg/L without; a UK gastroenterology review uses below 100 µg/L with inflammation — together with transferrin saturation. Soluble transferrin receptor card: sTfR rises in iron deficiency and tends to be normal in anemia of inflammation, so a raised sTfR or sTfR/log ferritin index suggests added absolute deficiency; assays are not standardized and cut-offs are method-dependent. Hook answers: A = iron deficiency; B = anemia of inflammation; C = possible combined deficiency (ferritin 60 is below the WHO inflammation threshold) — check sTfR or the index.

cues.text: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so inflammation can lift it into the normal range even when stores are running low.
So check C-reactive protein, and when inflammation is present raise the ferritin threshold: the WHO uses below seventy micrograms per litre in adults with inflammation, instead of below fifteen.

Soluble transferrin receptor rises in iron deficiency and tends to stay normal in anemia of inflammation. A raised receptor, or a raised receptor to log ferritin index, suggests added true deficiency, but the assays are not standardized.

Back to the hook. Patient A has iron deficiency. Patient B has anemia of inflammation. Patient C’s ferritin of sixty looks normal, but with active inflammation it sits below the WHO threshold, so combined deficiency is possible and the receptor tests can help.

lines: Acute-phase rise can mask low stores

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal ferritin rules out iron deficiency” (✓ inflammation raises ferritin; use an inflammation-adjusted threshold and CRP); “Low serum iron means iron deficiency” (✓ serum iron and saturation are low in both; stores decide); “Anemia of chronic disease is always microcytic” (✓ usually normocytic, sometimes microcytic).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal ferritin rules out iron deficiency. No: inflammation raises ferritin, so check CRP and use an adjusted threshold.
Trap two: low serum iron means iron deficiency. No: serum iron and saturation are low in both. Ferritin and transferrin decide.
Trap three: anemia of chronic disease is always microcytic. No: it is usually normocytic, and only sometimes microcytic.

scenes.title: Empty pantry, locked pantry
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Iron deficiency is an EMPTY pantry: the shelf gauge (ferritin) reads low and extra delivery trucks (transferrin) circle looking for iron. Anemia of inflammation is a LOCKED pantry: hepcidin holds the key, the gauge reads full, and fewer trucks run.” Tokens: empty = ferritin ↓, transferrin ↑ · locked = ferritin normal/↑, transferrin normal/↓. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: iron deficiency is an empty pantry. The shelf gauge, ferritin, reads low, and extra delivery trucks, transferrin, circle looking for iron. Inflammation is a locked pantry: hepcidin holds the key, the gauge reads full, and fewer trucks run.

Where it breaks: inflammation pushes the gauge up by itself, so a full reading can hide an empty shelf; both problems can exist in the same patient; and red-cell size can overlap, because anemia of inflammation can be microcytic too.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Both: serum iron ↓ · saturation ↓ → read the stores”, “Empty: ferritin ↓ Tf ↑ · Locked: ferritin N/↑ Tf N/↓ · check CRP”.

cues.text: Serum iron and transferrin saturation are low in both iron deficiency and anemia of inflammation, so read the stores instead: low ferritin with raised transferrin means empty stores, while normal or high ferritin with normal or low transferrin means locked stores, and inflammation can lift ferritin enough to hide a true deficiency.

props.label: Both: serum iron ↓ · saturation ↓ → read the stores
Empty: ferritin ↓ Tf ↑ · Locked: ferritin N/↑ Tf N/↓ · check CRP

explanation.what: Plain language: in iron deficiency the body has run out of stored iron; in anemia of inflammation the iron is there but locked away where the marrow cannot use it. Scientific terms: iron deficiency anemia (IDA), anemia of inflammation or anemia of chronic disease (ACD/AI), serum ferritin, transferrin and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), transferrin saturation (TSAT), red cell distribution width (RDW), hepcidin, soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR), sTfR/log ferritin index, stainable marrow iron.
explanation.why: Inflammation raises hepcidin, which blocks iron release from macrophages and absorption from the gut, so iron is diverted into storage while the marrow is starved. Ferritin is a positive acute-phase protein and rises with inflammation; transferrin is a negative acute-phase protein and falls. In true deficiency, stores empty first and transferrin rises.
explanation.measure: Both: serum iron and TSAT low. IDA: ferritin low (WHO: < 15 µg/L in adults without inflammation), transferrin/TIBC raised, RDW raised, microcytic hypochromic. ACD: ferritin normal or high, transferrin/TIBC normal or low, RDW typically normal, usually mild-to-moderate normocytic (can be microcytic). With inflammation (raised CRP): WHO threshold < 70 µg/L in adults; a UK gastroenterology review uses < 100 µg/L with TSAT. sTfR rises in iron deficiency and tends to be normal in ACD; sTfR/log ferritin helps detect combined deficiency but assays are not standardized. Absent stainable marrow iron is the traditional gold standard for absolute deficiency; marrow is not done routinely.
explanation.differs: Empty stores (IDA: ferritin ↓, transferrin ↑, RDW ↑) vs locked stores (ACD: ferritin normal/↑, transferrin normal/↓, RDW normal) vs combined IDA plus ACD (ferritin in the normal range with inflammation, raised sTfR or sTfR/log ferritin index).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the iron-study pattern for IDA or ACD, recognise that low serum iron and TSAT occur in both, identify the gold-standard test (marrow iron stain), and explain why an inflamed patient’s normal ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency.

comparisons.title: Iron deficiency vs anemia of inflammation
comparisons.distinguisher: Stores: ferritin and transferrin move in opposite directions in the two conditions, while serum iron and saturation are low in both.

comparisons.title: Reading ferritin with and without inflammation

left.label: No inflammation
points: WHO: < 15 µg/L = iron deficiency in adults

right.label: Inflammation (CRP ↑)
points: Ferritin raised as an acute-phase protein
WHO: < 70 µg/L in adults; add TSAT, sTfR/log ferritin

comparisons.distinguisher: Check CRP before trusting a “normal” ferritin.

mnemonic.text: Iron deficiency is an EMPTY pantry: the shelf gauge (ferritin) reads low and extra delivery trucks (transferrin) circle looking for iron. Anemia of inflammation is a LOCKED pantry: hepcidin holds the key, the gauge reads full, and fewer trucks run.
mnemonic.explanation: Ferritin = stores gauge, transferrin = delivery trucks, hepcidin = lock.
mnemonic.limitation: Inflammation raises ferritin by itself, so a full gauge can hide an empty shelf; both conditions can coexist; red-cell size can overlap because anemia of inflammation is sometimes microcytic.

analogyLimitations: Scenario and its values are invented.
Ferritin thresholds differ between guidelines and populations; assays differ.
takeaway: Serum iron and transferrin saturation are low in both iron deficiency and anemia of inflammation, so read the stores instead: low ferritin with raised transferrin means empty stores, while normal or high ferritin with normal or low transferrin means locked stores, and inflammation can lift ferritin enough to hide a true deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia has low serum iron, low transferrin saturation, low serum ferritin, raised TIBC and a raised RDW. Which condition best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. Low ferritin shows empty stores, and raised TIBC (transferrin) and RDW fit iron deficiency.
Incorrect. Ferritin is normal or high and TIBC normal or low in anemia of inflammation.
Incorrect. High ferritin with a transferrin saturation above about 45% prompts evaluation for iron overload; here ferritin and saturation are both low.
Incorrect. Nothing in the stem suggests inflammation, and a low ferritin already shows depleted stores; masking is a concern when inflammation lifts ferritin into the normal range.

questions.stem: Which pair of results is LEAST useful for separating iron deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disease?

options.rationale: Correct. Both are low in iron deficiency and in anemia of inflammation.
Incorrect. These usually move in opposite directions in the two conditions (ferritin ↓/TIBC ↑ vs ferritin normal-↑/TIBC normal-↓).
Incorrect. Absent stainable iron is the traditional gold standard for absolute deficiency; iron is present in anemia of inflammation.

options.text: Soluble transferrin receptor and the sTfR/log ferritin index
options.rationale: Incorrect. sTfR rises in iron deficiency and tends to be normal in anemia of inflammation, although assays are not standardized.

questions.stem: A woman with active Crohn disease and a raised C-reactive protein has microcytic anemia and a serum ferritin of 55 µg/L. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Iron deficiency is still possible, because inflammation raises ferritin; this value is below the WHO inflammation threshold of 70 µg/L
options.rationale: Correct. Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so thresholds are raised when inflammation is present.

options.text: Iron deficiency is excluded because ferritin is above 15 µg/L
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 15 µg/L cut-off applies to adults without inflammation.

options.text: The ferritin cannot be interpreted at all during inflammation
options.rationale: Incorrect. It can be interpreted with an adjusted threshold and supporting tests such as TSAT and sTfR.

options.text: The result indicates iron overload from inflammation
options.rationale: Incorrect. A ferritin of 55 µg/L is not hyperferritinemia; high ferritin with transferrin saturation above about 45% is what prompts evaluation for iron overload.

Ferritin is an acute-phase protein; WHO thresholds as summarized here (< 15 µg/L in adults, cited to WHO 2022; < 70 µg/L in adults with inflammation, WHO 2020); TSAT recommended particularly in chronic inflammation; RDW increase typical in IDA; absent stainable marrow iron as traditional gold standard, stainable iron in functional deficiency, marrow not routine; sTfR/log ferritin ratio useful in inflammation, limited by availability and differing assay thresholds.

claims.text: Hepcidin blocks macrophage iron release and gut absorption; iron diverted into storage; ferritin positive and transferrin negative acute-phase proteins.
Serum iron and TSAT are low in both IDA and anemia of inflammation.
IDA: ferritin low, transferrin/TIBC raised, RDW raised, microcytic hypochromic.
ACD: ferritin normal/high, transferrin/TIBC normal/low, RDW normal, usually mild-to-moderate normocytic, sometimes microcytic.
Absent stainable marrow iron is the traditional gold standard for absolute deficiency; iron present in functional deficiency; marrow not routine.
Inflammation can mask iron deficiency; check CRP; WHO < 70 µg/L in inflamed adults (< 15 µg/L otherwise); < 100 µg/L in a UK gastroenterology review.
claims.note: WHO thresholds taken from the summary in Iolascon 2024; the WHO guideline itself was not opened in this session.

claims.text: sTfR rises in iron deficiency and tends to be normal in AI; sTfR/log ferritin index helps detect combined deficiency; not standardized.
Reviewer Number Vault RDW interval (12–17%) and any RDW cut-off for separating IDA from ACD.
claims.note: Not taught; no open source read in this session gives these values.

claims.text: Scenario and values invented; iron-traffic diagram schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 9 Hit 1 says IDA and ACD are both microcytic. Nairz 2016 describes anemia of inflammation as typically a mild-to-moderate normocytic anemia that may be microcytic or normocytic; the lesson teaches “usually normocytic, sometimes microcytic” (register flag rv-acd-normocytic-ch9).

Ch. 9 Trap 1 tells the reader to pair ferritin with RDW and iron studies. The open sources read here instead adjust the ferritin threshold when inflammation is present (WHO 2020 as summarized by Iolascon 2024: < 70 µg/L in adults; Kumar 2022: < 100 µg/L), measure CRP, and use TSAT and sTfR/log ferritin to detect combined deficiency; the lesson teaches that approach (register flag rv-ferritin-inflammation-ch9).
